17 photos
Photo: SH Proshots
BMW has several new models in the making, and one of them is the range-topping version of the latest i3 Sedan, namely the M3 Electric .
This is what it should be called, as the Munich-based auto marque reportedly went for this name rather than christen it the i3 M or the iM3 because the automaker wanted enthusiasts to know that this is a real M car. Therefore, it has some big shoes to fill, because the M3 has always been a great driver’s car, regardless of the generation, so petrolheads have huge expectations when it comes to the driving part of the first-ever M3 Electric.
Despite the fact that we have encountered various prototypes of the upcoming BMW M3 Electric on several occasions, and that the model has also been teased, and has also fallen into the hands of the rendering crowd, its specifications remain a well-guarded secret. Nevertheless, reports indicate that it will feature a quad-motor setup with all-wheel drive, and from here on, you’ll get contradicting data if you try to look up the output.
That’s because while some believe that this model might offer in the region of 700 horsepower, others claim that around 800 horsepower is a more realistic figure. And there are also those who would argue that a four-digit output could also be a thing. After all, the platform, which is the Neue Klasse NAx, definitely supports this much power. However, we really would not hold our breath for roughly 1,000 horsepower or so.
Photo: SH Proshots Actually, not at first, anyway, because further down the line, BMW’s M Division could launch a CS version of the M3 Electric in order to make it more appealing, and it is this one that might get close or perhaps enter the four-digit realm. That’s my opinion, and you should take it with a pinch of salt. Realistically speaking, some 800 horsepower seems possible After all, it will take a swing at the Mercedes-AMG C-Class Electric, which is said to have a tri-motor setup with approximately 800 horsepower.
Our spies have read some recent reports that spoke about an estimated 850 horsepower, so they believe that this will be the output of the BMW M3 Electric, which is understood to tip the scales at roughly 2.3 metric tons, or over 5,000 pounds. The battery pack should have a capacity of around 100 kWh, enabling a rumored 650 km (400+ miles) or so range on the WLTP cycle, and supposedly charging at up to 420 kW. Adding up to 350 km (217 miles) of range might take around 10 minutes or so.
Keep in mind that the outputs mentioned in the above paragraphs are in metric horsepower, as the companies are European, they are testing these models on the other side of the Atlantic Ocean. However, as you already know, they will touch down in the United States of America . When will that happen? Probably sometime next year when it comes to both of them. Or at least that is when they are expected to premiere.
In the meantime, we will keep encountering prototypes in the open, and the pixel-altering crowd will keep having its way with them, though the BMW M3 Electric is definitely getting a lot more attention than its rival from the Affalterbach brand. And this story is also about it, as the scoops shared in the gallery just ended up in our inboxes, with our spy photographer managing to immortalize the prototype in question as it was being driven on public roads.
Photo: SH Proshots Due to the quite trippy camouflage, it stood out immediately, and we can clearly see that it looks pretty much like a toned down version of the BMW M Concept Neue Klasse unveiled earlier this year. And it’s not exactly a surprise, because we expected that. We can see a similar take when it comes to the front and rear bumpers, as well as the front hood, and other parts of the exterior.
The BMW M3 Electric appears to have wider tracks compared to the lesser i3 Sedan, on which it builds, and we expect a few changes on the inside too. There, the front seats should offer more lateral support, likely featuring integrated headrests. Exclusive trim and upholstery, as well as some carbon fiber inserts, should be part of the M makeover of the i3 Sedan, alongside dedicated load screens and submenus for the displays, including the Panoramic iDrive that stretches at the bottom of the windshield.
We still have plenty of things to find out about the first-ever BMW M3 Electric , and we expect the upcoming scooped testers to gradually start losing camouflage as the testing and fine-tuning phase of this model advances. As previously mentioned, the unveiling might take place next year, and it should hit our shores either for the 2027 or maybe the 2028 model year. We lean on the latter rather than the former.

Identification Friend or Foe (IFF) technology is a critical tool for quickly and accurately identifying friendly assets in a cluttered battlespace. (Photo illustration courtesy of BAE Systems.)
Identification Friend or Foe (IFF) technology has been around for decades, but as threats and platforms rapidly evolve, IFF must be adaptable to distinguish allied forces from potential threats and operate in contested and denied environments.
Breaking Defense spoke with Seth Guanu, Combat Identification Products program area director at BAE Systems , about how IFF technology is changing, how it can be used across both U.S. and allied forces, and how it must adapt to meet future threats.
Breaking Defense: IFF technology has been around for a long time. How is it critical to joint forces operations today?
Guanu: IFF is a question-and-answer system. It uses a waveform, which is electrical energy, to transmit data. If you’re a platform and you’re unsure of another platform’s friend status, you ask a question – which is called an interrogation – and the unknown platform responds via secure communications to positively identify itself. Interrogators ask the question, transponders answer the question, and combined interrogator transponders do both. We have these systems on aircraft, ships, land, and radar platforms.
Seth Guanu, Combat Identification Products program area director at BAE Systems
When you look back on history, the introduction of radar was revolutionary. However, radar only showed that something was out there, not whether it was friendly. There needed to be some way of identifying friendly forces where you weren’t spoofed by the enemy. IFF was introduced in World War II and continues to be a critical system.
IFF works alongside radars, data links, sensors and many other systems. For instance, if an adversary attempts to attack our assets from the air, IFF allows our defensive measures to engage threats without endangering friendly forces.
Since that time, warfare has expanded into multiple domains, not only land and sea and air, but space and cyber. Today’s adversaries are more agile and with new technology the speed of conflict has increased dramatically.
When you bring in unmanned systems and associated swarms it adds further complexity beyond what our forces have had to deal with in the past. The Department of War’s Joint All Domain Command and Control strategy (JADC2) strategy helps manage this by connecting assets across domains.
IFF underpins the C2 part of the strategy. This allows joint forces to sense and make sense of data. Is it friend or foe? Then you need to act. You need to be able to do that in split seconds, or you’re not ahead of the adversaries.
With changing threats, such as the proliferation of drones, how is IFF evolving to meet that challenge?
Modern warfare demands technological advances including enhanced cryptology, faster processing, and detection at greater ranges. IFF must be easily upgradeable to meet future threats.
Migrating to software-based IFF skills and card-based solutions is key to providing agility. Our IFF systems use a modular design and open system architecture that allows new capabilities to be integrated through software updates rather than hardware changes. This reduces obsolescence and accelerates enhancements without modifying fleet infrastructure.
Additionally, as unmanned air systems (UAS) expand in threat environments, new technologies are needed to equip the platforms that don’t overload the already crowded IFF frequency band. We are developing this technology and working with the IFF community to define enhancements to Mode 5 to address these changes to the combat environment.
As threats rapidly evolve, reliable IFF technology is critical for the US and its allies. (Video courtesy of BAE Systems.)
How can IFF be used across both U.S. and allied forces? What are the challenges to ensuring that IFF is being used effectively across joint forces and across all domains?
If you look at IFF or at these missions, say across the U.S. and its coalition, what are the things that you want? You want interoperability and standardization for U.S. and allied operations. Mode 5, the latest secure IFF waveform, is a NATO standard and supports worldwide interoperability.
The challenges associated with ensuring the effective use of Mode 5 across joint forces come from the significant number of different nations, platforms and manufacturers deploying unique IFF systems. In the U.S., the Air Traffic Control Radar Beacon System (ATCRBS), Identification Friend or Foe (IFF), and Mark XII Systems (AIMS) office ensures compatibility across U.S. and NATO forces.
Certifying equipment at both the box level and platform level is critical to overall system performance. The recent AIMS box-level certification of our AN/APX-127(V)1 Combined Interrogator Transponder is a major milestone. The new CIT provides advanced, multi-function capabilities while supporting the latest crypto and cybersecurity resilience requirements. The AIMS certification means the product is ready for use and can serve as a drop-in replacement for current systems.
In addition to having the same tools and waveform, everyone must operate under a consistent concept of operations (CONOPS), otherwise interoperability breaks down and then challenges can occur.
What are the benefits of a combined system and how does it differ from a standalone interrogator or transponder?
Ships typically use interrogators as a key element of their combat ID system to identify airborne objects while aircraft generally carry transponders to respond to questions.
A combined interrogator transponder (CIT) provides both capabilities in one box. This is essential for tactical aircraft that need to engage and where space for equipment is limited on the platform.
By combining both functions, CITs reduce size, weight and power demands and require only a single supporting infrastructure. Whether a platform uses an interrogator, transponder, or both depends on the mission and CONOPS.
How do you work around concerns about things such as jamming and spoofing?
IFF is a radio frequency (RF)-based solution, which can be subject to electronic warfare (EW) attacks. There’s constant evolution with RF so staying ahead of threats is crucial.
We are one of the key co-architects of the secure Mode 5 waveform, and our systems employ anti-jam techniques to operate in this contested environment.
We’re constantly maturing our technology, to support the latest crypto, anti-jam and cybersecurity resilient requirements. At a recent AIMS User Working Group, we successfully demonstrated our latest transponder’s resilience by introducing live RF jamming during the demo.
How long has BAE Systems been involved with IFF? What are your key areas of focus in IFF as you look forward?
BAE Systems has more than 80 years of IFF experience. Since Mode 5’s introduction in the mid-2000s, we have delivered more than 1,500 interrogators, 6,000 combined interrogator-transponder systems and 16,000 transponders across 140 platform types in more than 40 countries. Our systems support U.S. and coalition forces and air defense, weapons systems, air traffic control, and range instrumentation.
We develop solutions to outpace modern threats. We’ve seen a huge improvement in capability driving advanced performance while reducing size, weight and power. Modular firmware and software-defined architectures enable upgrades and integration into next-generation platforms.
Adversaries are agile so we must be faster by anticipating threats, developing counter technology and fielding updates quickly. Our next-generation products are designed as drop-in upgrades. With robust hardware processing capability, we can constantly update firmware and software after deployment to provide a new capability to address new threats.
Our enhancements, such as anti-jam and cyber resilience features, continue to lead in the industry. We’re listening to our customers. The future of IFF is a system that’s easily upgradeable, integrated, affordable and effective.
I’m proud to be part of the team at BAE Systems and our mission: “We Protect Those Who Protect Us.” We remain committed to delivering systems that meet today’s requirements and can rapidly adapt to tomorrow’s challenges.

At the 2026 Clinical Trials on Alzheimer’s Disease conference, AriBio reported that AR1001 slowed cognitive decline more than placebo in patients not taking other drugs for the disease.
AriBio’s Alzheimer’s asset hit one of the dual endpoints in a Phase 3 trial, slowing cognitive decline by 31% when used as a monotherapy.
The study, POLARIS-AD , randomized 1,535 patients with early Alzheimer’s to receive AR1001 or placebo once daily for 52 weeks. The dual primary endpoints assessed the change from baseline to week 52 on a scale for evaluating clinical decline in Alzheimer’s patients. One primary analysis included all patients, while the other focused on participants who did not take other Alzheimer’s medicines during the study.
AR1001, an oral therapy, is designed to drive neuroprotective effects by inhibiting PDE5, the same mechanism used by Viagra to relax smooth muscle cells and increase blood flow. PDE5 inhibitor use has been linked with lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease in large retrospective analyses.
AriBio’s drug candidate outperformed placebo at slowing decline in the monotherapy population, as measured by its primary endpoints. For trials designed with dual endpoints, only one needs to be met for the trial to succeed.
The treatment difference in the 604-patient subpopulation was −0.44 points versus placebo, representing a 31% slowing of clinical decline, the biotech reported Monday at the 2026 Clinical Trials on Alzheimer’s Disease (CTAD) conference. This population excluded patients who were receiving an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor or memantine at baseline.
In the overall population, the biotech’s drug candidate was not tied to a statistically significant effect. The treatment difference was −0.11 points versus placebo, or a 7% slowing of decline, that was not statistically significant.

“We started developing AR1001 with the goal of creating an oral treatment that could slow Alzheimer’s progression and be practical for patients and care partners to use over the long term,” AriBio CEO Jai-Jun Choung said in a prepared statement. “The 31% slowing of clinical decline at one year in the monotherapy population supports our hypothesis.”
The monotherapy result is in line with data on Biogen and Eisai’s Leqembi and Eli Lilly’s Kisunla, anti-amyloid drugs that slow disease progression. Leqembi achieved a −0.45-point CDR-SB treatment difference versus placebo, or 27% slower decline, at month 18 of the Phase 3 Clarity AD trial. Lilly, meanwhile, linked Kisunla to a −0.7-point CDR-SB treatment difference versus placebo, or 29% slower decline, at week 76 of its Phase 3 TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 trial.
AriBio intends to discuss the results with the FDA. Fosun Pharma, which in May paid $60 million for an option on AR1001, plans to further analyze and evaluate the results before deciding whether to exercise its right to license the drug candidate.
Secondary cognitive and functional measures numerically favored AR1001 in both populations. As in the primary analysis, the gap between AR1001 and placebo on the secondary endpoints was widest in the monotherapy group.
In that population, AR1001 had a non-significant treatment difference of −1.16 points over placebo on the Alzheimer’s Disease Assessment Scale–Cognitive Subscale 13, as well as a significant 0.7-point treatment difference versus placebo on the Mini-Mental State Examination. Cerebrospinal fluid levels of cyclic guanosine monophosphate, an intracellular messenger affected by PDE5 inhibitors, were significantly higher in the AR1001 arm than the placebo cohort in both the monotherapy group and the overall population.
As for safety, diarrhea was more common on AR1001 than placebo, affecting 7.7% and 4.4% of participants, respectively, and contributed to a higher rate of discontinuations due to adverse events in the treatment arm. The adverse event–related discontinuation rate was 5.2% on AR1001, versus 1.7% on placebo.
AriBio’s press release makes no mention of amyloid related imaging abnormalities (ARIA), a type of brain swelling associated with Leqembi and Kisunla. No ARIA-like symptoms or serious adverse events were seen in AriBio’s Phase 2 study, informing researchers’ belief that AR1001 may be an option for patients who do not tolerate or qualify for anti-amyloid therapies.

While most people are out looking for new TVs, laptops, and digital cameras, during Black Friday, I’m out here hunting down the best deals we can get our hands on. Well, here’s to e-biking and getting you mounted on a fresh budget and electrified steed ASAP.
With countless brands gearing up for Black Friday, I’ve decide to bring to light some of the brands that you should to have on your radar if you’re looking for an e-bike, be it for you or a loved one. While I’m only shedding light on just five of them, clearly, there are countless others that are also slashing prices, so take this list as a bit of a starting point, if you don’t already have one.
Engwe First up on our list of budget e-bike brands that are really unleashing all they have in terms of Black Friday goodness is none other than Engwe , the one and the same that sells all over the world. That said, the deals you can find from this crew do differ on where you are in the world.
Photo: Engwe For Europeans, one of the hottest deal that Engwe has in store is their Zip. It’s a folding e-bike that was designed to compete with Brompton, but at a fraction of the price. It was selling for €1,100 and is now up for grabs at a flat €1,000 ($1,100). If you’re wondering if you should pull the trigger on this one, keep in mind that 94 reviews have been left on the manufacturer’s website, amounting to a 5/5-star rating.
If you’re in the US, on the other hand, you can tap into the Eagle model, this brand’s electric pit bike, or pocket dirt bike. This model was selling for $1,200, but for Black Friday, this one’s flying off the shelf for a solid $800 (€750). A steal folks!
Other models are also under fire for Black Friday, actually, just about the entire Engwe lineup, marking it as the perfect time to pull the trigger on one of their e-bikes if you’ve been eyeing them.
Heybike Up next on our list of e-bike brands that are letting go of their monsters for less then ever, we have Heybike, a brand that has been on the market for quite some years, and while their e-bikes aren’t seeing massive price cuts on the same level as Engwe, they too have some considerable deals.
Photo: Heybike One important deal is the Ranger 3.0 Pro, going for $1,400 instead of $1,500, or the Mars 3.0, dropped from $1,200 to just $1,000. Again, not some massive price cuts, but Heybike already offers some decent deals, so going any lower is a bit tough.
Keep in mind that some of their dirt bikes are on sale, in particular the V1 and all it’s bundle deals and kits. The V1 Pro, however, is still going for its full price of $2,100 but does have the occasional price cut, so keep your eyes peeled for that one.
JaisonBike The name JasionBike is about as prolific as Engwe, and can be spotted selling all over the world too. Considering this crew has been on the market for ages too, they’re also able to really slash prices on their e-bikes.
One of their best deals is for their Hunter Pro, a fat tire ride going for just $960, down from $2,000. That’s over 50% off, and a clear budget ride to land on your e-bike radar. They’re X-Hunter is also a hot deal, dropped to just $880 from $1,900.
Photo: Jasionbike But, these two bikes are not alone. As mentioned, Jaison really went all out here, with rides like the Thunder Pro ST going for $1,200 from $1,900, and their Kago, a cargo e-bike, is at $800, down from $2,200, quite possibly, the best deal on their site, currently.
Duotts If there’s one brand that I noticed competing with some of the established giants on the market, it’s Duotts. This team came out of nowhere, with some rather questionable rides at first, but in time, turned into a serious crew to consider for a new e-bike.
In their lineup, the F26 and it’s Lite counterpart are a couple of deals worth considering. The standard F26 is selling under Black Friday for €1,250 ($1,380), down from €1,700. The Lite, on the other hand, is set for €1,050 ($1,150).
Photo: Duotts Just keep in mind that Duotts has really exploded in recent years, and even their more meaningful machines are seeing price cuts. One model in particular is the collab they did with 79Bike. The Falcon Pro is that model, but it’s a dirt bike, not pedal-powered, and it’s going for €380 less than before. It’s still a sizable price of €4,320 ($4,750) though, so don’t get too excited.
Himiway Last but not least, on this short list of budget e-bike names you need to be aware of, we have Himiway . One of the best deals this team has in store here is their A7 Pro Commuter. The bike normally goes for $2,900, but Himiway is letting it fly for just $2,000, and if I may, people who have ridden this bike call it the Rolls Royce of budget urban e-bikes, mainly because of the ultra-plush full-suspension and a mid-mounted motor.

Tesla is now taking orders for the $29,990 Cybercab, with the first deliveries expected in Austin next month. But there’s a problem buyers should know about: they won’t be able to charge it at home.
The Cybercab has no onboard charger, so it only takes DC fast charging. And the wireless home charging pad Tesla has been teasing since 2023 still isn’t something you can buy.
A DC-only car
When Tesla unveiled the Cybercab in 2024, Elon Musk said it wouldn’t even have a plug. “It just goes over the inductive charger and charges,” he said on stage.
That plan didn’t survive production, or at least the current version in production. Cybercabs have a NACS charge port behind a panel in the rear bumper, and Tesla has been plugging Cybercabs into regular Superchargers in Austin since they joined the fleet.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The bigger issue is what sits behind that port. Tesla confirmed to attendees at Tesla’s Austin launch event in September that Cybercab has no onboard charger, the box that turns the AC power coming out of your wall into DC power the battery can store.
No onboard charger means no Wall Connector. No Mobile Connector on a 120V outlet, and no Level 2 station at the mall either. If it isn’t a DC fast charger, the Cybercab can’t use it.
For a robotaxi, deleting the onboard charger makes sense. It’s one less part to buy, cool, and carry around, and a fleet car spends its downtime at a depot, not in someone’s garage. Those little things help make the car more economical and efficient.
But Tesla is now selling the Cybercab to individuals.
The fine print makes it worse
As we reported last week, Tesla’s Cybercab autonomy agreement requires a $299 monthly subscription for the car to move at all. The same document puts charging squarely on the buyer: “You are responsible for registration, insurance, parking, charging, general cleaning and all other costs.”
It also tells owners to “keep the vehicle charged and connected so over-the-air updates can install.” Connected to what, it doesn’t say.
The Cybercab Order Agreement limits the car to NACS DC fast charging, Superchargers included. It also says only the registered owner can use the Cybercab, and only while physically present in it for the entire trip.
The subscription agreement carves out one exception: when service is due, the Cybercab “will travel autonomously, unoccupied to a Tesla service center.” Nothing similar exists for charging.
So you can’t send your Cybercab to a Supercharger at 2 a.m. while you sleep, which is the one thing a self-driving car should be great at. You’d have to ride along, sit in a two-seater at a Supercharger while it charges, and ride back home.
Tesla has been teasing the fix for years
The obvious answer is the wireless home charger Tesla keeps promising.
Tesla first showed what looked like a wireless home charging station during its Investor Day in March 2023. Later that year, chief designer Franz von Holzhausen confirmed the project on Jay Leno’s Garage, saying owners would “just drive over the pad in your garage” to start charging.
Tesla then filed patents for the charging pad and, after the Cybercab unveiling, released a video of it charging the robotaxi at 25 kW, claiming efficiency “well above 90%.” In February, the FCC granted Tesla a waiver to use ultra-wideband radios to guide the Cybercab onto the pad.
And that’s where it stops. Tesla has never sold the pad, never priced it, and never given it a launch date. It even gave up on wireless charging for the Cybertruck last year, even though the truck shipped with the connectors for it.
With deliveries estimated for December, Tesla has about six weeks to launch a home pad if it wants the first owners to charge in their own garage.
The other options aren’t great
Tesla’s own plans for Cybercab charging revolve around fleet depots. In Austin, it filed plans for a hub on St. Elmo Road with 48 V4 Supercharger stalls in a first phase and cabinets to support 80 wireless chargers in a second.
Tesla could, in theory, let private owners use it. But with the owner-presence rule, that means riding to a depot across town and waiting there. That’s a Supercharger visit with extra steps.
The other route is a home DC charger, and those exist. We covered Sigenergy’s 25 kW bidirectional DC charging module last year, which bypasses a car’s onboard charger the same way a Supercharger does. Lunar Energy also announced a 25 kW home DC charger this year, but it’s not expected until mid-2027.
Neither is a plug-and-play answer. Sigenergy’s module is built to sit inside its SigenStor home battery system, which isn’t cheap, and Tesla would have to support third-party DC charging on a car it controls this tightly. Tesla could also build its own small DC wall unit. It hasn’t announced one, but CEO Elon Musk talked about integrating one into the Powerwall for years.
Electrek’s Take
This is what happens when you take a vehicle designed for a fleet and sell it to consumers to hit a deadline. And let’s be honest, charging is probably not even in the top 5 of problems with selling the Cybercab to personal owners in its current state.
Musk promised a Cybercab would be sold to a customer for under $30,000 before 2027. Technically, he’s going to make it. But on the Q3 earnings call, he also said “the vast majority” of Cybercabs will stay Tesla-owned and run as transport-as-a-service. The car was clearly engineered around that, and deleting the onboard charger is the best example.
That saved Tesla money on every unit. The cost now lands on the few people buying one.
If you live in Austin next to a Supercharger, you’ll manage. But think about what Tesla is actually selling here: a self-driving car that can’t drive itself to charge, can’t charge in your garage, and needs you sitting in it at a Supercharger. That’s worse than owning a Model 3 with a Wall Connector, and it costs $299 a month on top.
The fix exists in Tesla’s labs. It has the pad, the patents, and the FCC approval. It needs to ship it as a product, ideally bundled with the car, or change the contract to let the Cybercab go charge on its own.
Will the first Cybercab owners get a wireless pad in December, or will they spend their evenings at Superchargers? And if it launches, how much will it cost? The rare few home wireless chargers that have been sold to date have been quite expensive, and the value proposition of the Cybercab, which is currently basically a $300 a month lease with a $30,000 down payment, is already pretty awful.
If you’re buying an EV, how you charge it at home matters as much as the car itself, and pairing it with rooftop solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero. Bentley's Torcal EV Pushes New Orders Into 2028 Before Production Begins
56 photos
Photo: Bentley
Love it or hate it, the Torcal has a problem that Bentley is glad for. According to chief executive officer Frank-Steffen Walliser, customers putting an order on the British automaker's first electric vehicle today have to wait until 2028 for delivery. Speaking to Automotive News, the big kahuna hasn't disclosed how many units are in the offing for 2027.
At the end of the day, the entire first-year allocation has been spoken for, and that's really good news for the model that many among us criticized for being a Porsche Cayenne Electric with a nicer cabin and more in-your-face styling. In a similar fashion to the Ferrari Luce, the Torcal simply does not care about the rational naysayers and the bona fide haters.
The Volkswagen Group-controlled manufacturer intends to start production in the first half of 2027, with Crewe serving as the stomping ground of the Torcal. Before criticizing the company for taking a little too much from public debut to the start of series production, bear in mind this is the company's first electric vehicle and the first EV to be assembled in Crewe.
Selling out for 2027 also indicates that Bentley was right when it decided that there is enough room for a battery-electric model in this very expensive corner of the market, alongside a plethora of internal combustion models. The Torcal is joined by the Continental GT twins, Flying Spur, and the Bentayga in the automaker's core model lineup, with all of them being assembled in Crewe rather than at Volkswagen Group sites across Europe.
It's also worth noting that Bentley was right to position the Torcal below the Bentayga price-wise. A little over $220,000 gets you the most basic of specifications in the United States of America for model year 2028, whereas the base version of the Bentayga is nearly $10,000 pricier.
For anyone expecting an affordable entry into Bentley ownership, neither product can be considered entry-level despite their Cayenne Electric and Cayenne underpinnings.
Photo: Bentley Walliser told Automotive News that Bentley 's electric vehicle has attracted plenty of youngsters and customers who are completely new to the brand, and this matters a lot in the long run. The early preference for the high-output Torcal S is another interesting detail shared by Walliser.
Instead of the standard 810 horsepower and a ridiculous 852 pound-feet (1,155 Newton-meters) of twist, S buyers get to enjoy 876 horsepower and 996 pound-feet (1,350 Newton-meters) when launch control is used. The S also happens to be quicker and faster. Both rely on a 113.2-kWh battery that delivers a maximum driving range of 373 miles (600 kilometers), and both support 400-kW charging.
That means 16 minutes are required in optimal conditions to get the high-voltage battery from 10 to 80 percent. Capable of sprinting to 60 miles per hour (97 kilometers per hour) in 2.8 seconds, the S version tops 162 miles per hour (260 kilometers per hour) despite being listed with direct drive instead of a two-speed tranny for the rear-mounted drive unit.
Walliser further shared that Torcal and Torcal S customers are willing to spend well beyond sticker. Speaking to Automotive News, he acknowledged that some configurations exceed 300,000 pounds sterling, which is extremely close to 400,000 dollars at current exchange rates.

source_document.body:
MANILA, Philippines — Top officials from Australia and the Philippines have inked a defense pact to accelerate military coordination, paving the way for rotational troop deployment and Australian investments in Philippine military infrastructure.
The Nov. 15 Defense Cooperation Agreement, or DCA, is designed to cut administrative bottlenecks and create a more efficient coordination system to fast-track bilateral defense activities.
So far the two countries’ military exchanges have largely fallen under a 1995 memorandum of agreement, while troop exchanges were guided by the Status of Visiting Forces Agreement, signed in 2007 and effective since 2012.
According to Australia’s Department of Defence, the new pact covers intelligence-sharing, military training, the transfer of aerial and surface drones, maritime activities, and military infrastructure.
“This new Defence Cooperation Arrangement will deepen practical cooperation between our defense forces and create new opportunities to work together in support of regional security,” Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said in a statement.
Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. said the new DCA reduces bureaucratic barriers, particularly in troop deployment, and would allow Australia to rapidly deploy troops to aid in Philippine disaster response.
“Rather than 100 steps to do a single thing, it will just now take 10 … and it will be more purposeful and not ad hoc,” Teodoro told reporters following the signing.
The move comes as Australia recalibrates its defense posture in response to China’s expanding military capabilities, growing missile reach, and increasing use of gray-zone tactics and economic coercion in the Indo-Pacific.
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. (C) and First Lady Louise Araneta-Marcos (R) welcome Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese ahead of the Gala Dinner during the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila on Nov. 16, 2026. (Nhac Nguyen / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)
“From Australia’s point of view, the Philippines is our first line of defense,” Australian Strategic Policy Institute senior fellow Euan Graham told Defense News.
Australia has experienced harassment by PLA forces, including dangerous maritime maneuvers, laser targeting in its northern exclusive economic zone, and the use of sonar and flares in close proximity to Royal Australian Navy vessels.
Like Australia, the Philippines faces Chinese pressure head-on. Chinese ships have used high-powered water cannons, pointed military-grade lasers, rammed, and attacked Armed Forces of the Philippines vessels and personnel.
When asked if the DCA was meant to boost deterrence in the Taiwan Strait, Teodoro emphasized the agreement will bolster “deterrence in the West Philippine Sea” and in “Philippine territory.”
Strategy shift
Australia marked a historic peacetime shift toward a strategy of denial in 2023, most recently codified in the 2026 national defense strategy.
The idea is to reshape the Australian Defense Force into an integrated, focused military capable of deterring and denying access to its northern approaches, which includes deploying a forward-defense force.
Earlier this year, Australia created the new Littoral Maneuver Group under the 18th Sustainment Brigade headquartered in Brisbane, to operate farther north, making the Philippines an important part of that strategy.
But Australia can only deploy small units, analyst Graham cautioned. And keeping these mobile forces supplied and operational in archipelagic countries like the Philippines is challenging, as troops and equipment are moved across widely dispersed islands during operations.
Building logistics networks
To that end, the new cooperation agreement is expected to facilitate discussions on potential Australian investments in Philippine military infrastructure.
A list of five Luzon bases slated to receive funding for eight infrastructure projects was expected to be finalized around August this year. However, only one base has been discussed in detail so far, officials told Defense News.
Teodoro previously clarified that base agreements with Australia will follow a different model than the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA) between the Philippines and the United States, which includes provisions for prepositioning military equipment and assets.
The Australian “basing” arrangements, officials said, would include areas that are not traditional bases.
Rather than a large basing presence, what the Australian military needs is access to locations that could sustain its forces during operations and contingencies.
Discussions so far have included sustainment and logistics to support joint operations while troops spread across the archipelago’s most complex, most challenging, and remote terrains.
Graham said Australia’s role in the Philippines is distinct but complementary to that of the United States. While physical locations could overlap, the infrastructure projects would be different.
Canberra and Manila in 2021 signed the Mutual Support Logistics Arrangement, which covers fuel and other supplies for aircraft and vessels, transportation, logistics, and coordination.
“The importance of logistics can’t be underestimated. It’s not just about getting your fighting force fighting. You’ve got to supply them with food, fuel, and ammunition during all of that,” Graham said.
More complex training
With the new DCA with Australia in place, joint exercises , especially Exercise ALON, will see a larger iteration next year, Teodoro said.
Exercise ALON, first held in 2023, is the biennial flagship joint training exercise between countries, focused on amphibious operations.
The 2025 edition saw Australia’s largest overseas military exercise for the year and showcased the ADF projecting combat forces into the contested West Philippine Sea, Graham said.
Apart from maritime training, Teodoro said there will be more aerial, land, cyber, and multidomain training exercises between Filipino and Australian troops.
Military officials told Defense News that Army training has been a priority area for the Australian military’s training playbook in the Philippines. The focus follows sweeping changes in both countries’ land forces to prepare them for modern conflicts.
While the Philippine Army expands from its signature jungle and urban warfare expertise toward coastal defense, the Australian ground service has pivoted toward littoral warfare.
Since 2023, exchanges have focused on techniques, tactics, and procedures for amphibious operations, Army spokesperson Col. Louie Dema-ala told Defense News.
But future iterations will include advanced training, Dema-ala said. “We are transitioning into a multi-domain capable Army.”
The exchange is not one-sided. Australia also stands to benefit from the Philippine Army’s experience operating in dense jungle terrain.
“This is not just a one-way process. We can learn from the jungle warfare fighting skills, and I think that’s important to stress. No one can tell us about the Philippines better than the Filipinos,” Graham said.

source_document.body:
For much of the past three years, freight was cheap enough to ignore. Shippers could lean on the spot market , push problems downstream, and skip the hard conversations about how their networks were built. That window has closed. As shippers finalize 2027 budgets, climbing transportation costs, tariff uncertainty, and a new Congress taking shape are forcing questions many had put off.
Chuck Papa, president of transportation management at NFI , has watched the shift happen in real time. With roughly 30 years in the industry, he says the current moment stands out. Geopolitics, Papa said, has been “the biggest roller coaster of impact we’ve probably seen since the 30 years I’ve been doing this.”
Rate volatility returns to the boardroom
The most common question NFI hears from customers planning for next year is what the market will do. The era of not worrying about rates, Papa said, is behind shippers. Because tariffs and policy remain unpredictable, NFI is steering customers toward flexibility. “Let’s be resilient and flexible, so we can deal with these as they occur,” he said.
Rising costs are also changing who is paying attention. “When transportation rates are low, nobody thinks about the overall cost,” Papa said. But “over the last six months, rates have gone up dramatically,” and that has put transportation spending in front of board-level executives who had not been asking about it. The result, according to Papa, is a broader conversation about the cost of the entire supply chain, not just the freight bill.
The spot market hangover
One of the clearest consequences of the freight recession is what happened to carrier relationships. Papa said shippers who have leaned heavily on the spot market have felt the most pain. “A lot of the shippers that have played the spot market didn’t really maintain relationships with carriers, and they’re now paying the price,” he said.
The fix is neither complicated nor new. “We can’t move freight without carriers,” Papa said, so NFI has encouraged shippers to rebuild strategic relationships that slipped during the downturn. That also means avoiding the opposite extreme. “You don’t want to have too many carriers either,” he said, since spreading volume too thin weakens the leverage a shipper has with any one of them.
Papa said the performance gap shows up in the data. As an example, he pointed to payment: “We’ll never go beyond 30-day payment terms.” Many shippers, he added, still treat carrier selection as a procurement event rather than a strategic one. Newer logistics professionals face a learning curve too. “They have never dealt with a tight capacity market,” Papa said of those who entered the industry in the last three years.
Transportation doesn’t start at the dock
If rebuilding carrier relationships is the first priority, the second is looking upstream. Papa described a customer shipping LTL from a Greater Philadelphia facility to Southern California. The customer’s focus was getting freight out the door the moment it was available, and its teams, in Papa’s words, “focus on shipping, not delivery date.” NFI had long argued that holding and consolidating freight, using multi-stop truckload or a cross-dock, could improve both service and cost. With rates low, there was little appetite to hear it. Now, Papa said, the customer is willing to take the conversation across its organization.
That means revisiting basics such as minimum order quantities and correcting the transit times in customers’ ERP systems. “It is better planning and optimization,” Papa said, describing “that shift back to much more of a supply chain conversation versus just transportation.”
The lesson, as Papa framed it: “Transportation doesn’t start when the product becomes available on the dock. It starts much sooner.”
What separates strong partners from the rest
Asked what makes a carrier or partner worth keeping, Papa kept the answer simple. It is “those that will listen and collaborate,” and who stay flexible as carrier networks change. Some carriers simply can no longer serve a lane the way they once did, and the productive response is to find alternatives rather than insist the carrier fix it.
For shippers evaluating a managed transportation provider, Papa said the green flag is providers who expand the conversation beyond just transportation. Providers that raise supply chain issues beyond the dock door are the ones who can challenge a shipper’s thinking. The red flag is a provider more focused on its own assets or internal services than on the customer’s outcome. “If you have to constantly bring ideas to them, that to me is a red flag versus them bringing ideas to you,” he said.
The best providers, Papa added, act as “an extension of their customers,” often joining annual operating plan discussions. NFI also looks across its own book of business for matches that benefit both parties. “How can we network our customers together where there are synergies for them,” he said, citing backhaul opportunities as one example.
AI moves network design from annual to continuous
When it comes to data analysis, Papa pointed to AI. Traditionally, network design is a periodic project, often done about once a year. NFI has embedded AI into Vantage, its control tower, so the analysis runs continuously and flags changes to NFI’s operators, such as how the past four to six weeks compare with the same period a year earlier. Papa calls the approach “a dynamic freight network design versus static.”
Another example is the detection of a new lane that lacks a contracted rate. The system recognizes when volume on the lane is high enough to justify a mini bid and prompts a user to run one. That is the generative stage, Papa explained. The next stage is agentic: putting the bid out, procuring the carrier rate and updating the transportation management system automatically.
Papa doesn’t see this as displacing the people involved, calling it “an evolution.” The goal is to let operators act on changes as they happen, because by the time a quarterly review catches an issue, “it’s too late.” He expects “the days of doing annual or biannual network studies are going to be gone and replaced with a real-time network assessment.”
Why shippers outsource transportation management
Papa was also asked why a shipper should partner with a transportation management provider at all. For most companies, he said, logistics is a back-office function, while for NFI “it’s front office. It’s what we do and breathe every day.” He contrasted that with customers who adopt a TMS as software alone: after year one or two of good results, “it drops off because they don’t have the ability to retain, train, and continue to advance their capabilities.”
Scale also helps with seasonality. Papa said some NFI customers see huge spikes at certain times of year and then slow down. Rather than staffing to peak, “We’ve made that a design variable,” he said, adjusting technology and resources as demand changes.
The 2027 takeaway
Asked for one recommendation for shippers planning 2027, Papa gave two: build carrier relationships and “look beyond the dock.” Shippers that do both, he said, will be better positioned for whatever the market does next.

Seven in 10 manufacturing specialists still use spreadsheets or lists to track whether their products meet compliance requirements, according to a recent Assent study . Only 31% said they use software built specifically for product compliance.
What’s Related
The biggest reporting problem was the information itself. Fifty-seven percent cited incomplete or unreliable data as a major challenge in meeting product compliance and sustainability reporting requirements. Limited staffing came close behind at 53%, while 48% cited regulatory complexity.
Assent and Germany’s Pforzheim University surveyed 131 manufacturing specialists and managers from April through June 2026, including respondents in the automotive and electronics industries, and supplemented the survey with seven expert interviews.
Where supplier data falls short
The study looked at what happens when manufacturers ask suppliers for data on carbon emissions . Incomplete information and late responses tied as the most common problems, each cited by 55% of respondents. Forty-five percent said suppliers received unclear instructions about what data to provide, and 40% pointed to a lack of automation for submitting responses.
The report described how manufacturers can make those requests easier to answer. A request can spell out which parts it covers and what emissions the supplier should count. A common submission process can also spare suppliers from entering the same information in different formats.
RELATED STORIES: Manufacturers Say Supervisors Waste 4 Hours Per Shift on Data | 10 Routine Supply Chain Tasks You Should Use AI For
How much time manual work takes
Sixty-nine percent of respondents said they spent up to two hours a day on repetitive manual work, including 34% who reported spending one to two hours. Another 15% reported spending three to four hours a day on those tasks. About one-third described their current processes as efficient.
Spreadsheets were the most common tool, even though 58% reported using enterprise resource planning systems, the software companies use to manage functions such as purchasing and inventory. Respondents could select more than one tool, so a company could use a central system and still rely on spreadsheets for some compliance work.
AI draws interest, but no one is using it
AI and automation ranked as the biggest opportunity in the survey, but only 10% said they had built AI into their processes. Among respondents whose systems already shared data, 72% saw AI as an opportunity, compared with 48% of those whose systems were separate.
Technology and software led the list of investment priorities at 43%, followed by connecting data and IT systems at 35%. Assent said those connections matter because AI tools draw on records about parts, finished products, and suppliers. If those records are incomplete or kept in separate systems, the tools have less reliable information to work with.

By Alison Koo
17 November 2026
Charter prices for containerships continue to defy the cooldown in long-haul freight rates, as major operators continue to hunt tonnage.
Linerlytica this week reported that French line CMA CGM took the 2001-built 5,610 teu Aigio (previously known as Wan Hai 611 ) for 3.5 years.
While the rate was not disclosed, charter rates for similar-size vessels are around $66,000 a day, up 10% year on year.
Aigio is one of three sister ships Wan Hai sold in March for $34m to $38m each, Greek tonnage provider Costamare buying two and CMA CGM the other – Wan Hai 612 and Wan Hai 613 have not been renamed or delivered yet.
Charter rates for box ships of all sizes have risen by between 7% and 23% year on year, with feeder vessels registering the biggest gains due to higher demand from intra-region trades and the lack of newbuilds in recent years. A 1,700 teu ship is now going for around $32,000 a day.
“The strong demand in the containership charter market continues, with charter rates still edging upwards, with forward fixtures stretching into the end of 2027,” Linerlytica said.
CMA CGM has also been busy in the second-hand market, having bought the 2017-built 2,506 teu Nordamelia from Reederei Nord at an undisclosed price. Since 2020, the carrier has bought 178 ships, narrowing the capacity gap with Maersk to just 130,000 teu.
Meanwhile MSC, by far the busiest buyer of second-hand ships, continues to hunt for tonnage to consolidate its lead over its peers.
The Geneva-headquartered operator lately bought the 2011-built 5,550 teu MSC Cadiz , after chartering it from Claus-Peter Offen for 15 years, taking its fleet to 7.46m teu.
Since the pandemic sent freight and charter rates to historical highs, MSC has acquired 521 ships, for 1.6m teu.

It’s been a long road to financial stability for Genetix Biotherapeutics, the rebranded name of bluebird bio following its February 2025 sale to two private equity firms, but on Monday the biotech estimated full year 2026 sales will reach $500 million.
Genetix Biotherapeutics, the genetic medicine company formerly known as bluebird bio, has emerged from hibernation to report a 95% year-over-year increase in sales for key blood disease products like Lyfgenia and Zynteglo.
The company on Monday reported $327 million in U.S. net sales year to date, stemming from increased reimbursement for American patients. Genetix said that 700 patients have signed up for treatment since 2022, including 326 this year alone.
That compares to the dozens of patients who received infusions of Lyfgenia, Zynteglo or the company’s third marketed treatment Skysona in 2024.
Genetix reported net sales for 2026 to reach $500 million. This is great news for shareholders, who are due a contingent value right from the company’s new private equity owners if annual sales reach $600 million before December 31, 2027.
It’s been a long road to get there.
Back to basics
You may know Genetix as bluebird, the embattled company that received one of two historic approvals for a gene therapy in sickle cell disease in December 2023. Despite the medical and scientific advancement, bluebird struggled to market the therapy and the rest of its portfolio, which includes Zynteglo for beta thalassemia and Skysona for cerebral adrenoleukodystrophy (CALD).
Facing a cash crunch and a plummeting valuation, bluebird was sold to global investment firms Carlyle and SK Capital Partners for roughly $50 million in February 2025. The deal offered shareholders $3 per share in cash right away, plus a CVR equaling $6.84 per share if its current product portfolio achieves $600 million in net sales in any 12-month period before Dec. 31, 2027.

S&P Capital IQ currently values the potential earnout at about $68 million, which would be beyond the initial upfront payout to shareholders.
Bluebird went back to basics, rebranding to its old name —Genetix—and shifting its focus from cell and gene therapy to genetic medicines. Since then, the company has been mostly working in the background, save a few broad updates.
On Monday, the company was ready to show what had been happening behind the scenes.
“In just 18 months, we have transformed Genetix into a profitable, high-growth commercial enterprise, proving that genetic medicine can deliver both life-changing outcomes for patients and sustainable commercial success,” CEO David Meek said in a statement . “With approximately $500 million in expected 2026 U.S. net sales, an established hematology franchise, and significant untapped patient opportunity, we are only beginning to unlock our potential.”
During the 18-month period, Genetix enhanced and expanded its manufacturing network, expanded access to 100 qualified treatment centers in the U.S. and achieved reimbursement for more than 95% of U.S. patients, the company reported.
Manufacturing capacity was doubled, enhancing reliability of the network to 90%, up 20% since 2024, Genetix said. The number of cell collections required for developing each treatment has also declined, with 85% of patients getting enough cells with just two collections. The process has also been sped up by 25 days, with turnaround time now at 65 days.
On the commercial side, Genetix has seen growing demand as awareness rises, thanks to efforts such as a partnership with the National Football League Alumni Association.

Lygenia is also being expanded into the pediatric population. Dosing began in a clinical study called HGB-210 that includes children as young as 2 years, while a regulatory submission is planned for the end of the year to extend the age limit down to 12.
All these efforts have helped prepare Genetix for a global expansion to drive “multibillion-dollar growth,” Meek said. The company finally hit profitability in the fourth quarter of 2025 and that has continued ever since, according to the release. When public, bluebird repeatedly reported net losses, with the most recent hitting $200 million as reported in full year earnings for 2024. At that time, Genetix said that the three products combined for $83.8 million in sales.
When Genetix last provided an update on its strategic priorities in March , sales numbers were not provided for 2025. As a private company now, Genetix is not required to disclose financials.

This 2025 BMW M5 Failing To Sell for Over $93,000 Is Quite Interesting
16 photos
Photo: Cars & Bids
This 2025 BMW M5 only has 2,800 miles on the clock and recently failed to sell at auction where the highest anybody would bid was $93,000. The MSRP on this thing was $130,225, which goes to show just how rapidly the G90 M5 is depreciating once it leaves the showroom floor. This is great news for buyers, because they're getting a lot of car for the money.
Despite its controversial nature, the latest-generation BMW M5 is still a pretty awesome car. What's controversial about it, you ask? Come on - the weight gain, the plug-in hybrid powertrain, the polarizing design. You name it! The thing is, the plug-in hybrid system is actually one of its strong suits, and the design isn't bad at all, especially with those wider arches.
The result on this car is revealing, with the bidding maxing out at $93,000. It points to a tension between what the G90 M5 costs new and what at least some buyers are currently prepared to pay for a used one. People are extremely interested in bargain-hunting on this car, and it's easy to understand why. On paper, the new M5 is a beast, regardless of how much it weighs.
Now, if this was my car, given the mileage, I'm pretty sure I'd have held out too. It can still fetch more than $93,000. Not a lot more, but more. I absolutely love the Isle of Man Green Metallic exterior colorway. It's one of the best colors ever that you can spec on a fast Bimmer.
Other notable equipment includes the 20" and 21" Style 951M wheels, both the Carbon and Executive packages, the Driving Assistant Plus system, heated and ventilated front seats, heated rear seats, carbon fiber high gloss silver thread interior trim, a Bowers & Wilkins surround sound system, and more. I'm also a big fan of the Kyalami Orange and Black upholstery. It's the exact same spec I drove during my review of the G90 M5 back in 2025 - you can read all about it here .
Spoiler alert, great car. Absolutely tremendous feat of engineering. It's not as fun to drive as an M5 Comp but as an overall package, it just delivers on everything it promises.
Photo: Cars & Bids It all starts with the 4.4-liter twin-turbocharged V8 engine, working alongside an electric motor and a 14.8-kWh lithium-ion battery. The combined system output is 717 horsepower (727 ps) and 738 lb-ft (1,000 Nm) of torque. Everything gets sent to all four wheels via an 8-speed automatic transmission.
The new M5 can hit 60 mph (97 kph) in just 3.4 seconds, before maxing out at 190 mph (305 kph) with the optional M Driver's Pack. Furthermore, you can drive this car on electric power alone at speeds of up to 87 mph (140 kph), which means that you can literally use this as an EV 100% of the time, should you choose to (in favorable conditions, of course).
